h: Ten years of demonetisation: black money survived, the poor took the blow
dek: Economist Arun Kumar reminds us that the 2016 decision met none of its goals, and now the Andhra chief minister is talking about scrapping the 500 rupee note.
body: Arun Kumar, who taught economics at JNU and has written books on the black economy, reopens the old accounts as demonetisation turns ten. The reason is fresh: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu has suggested withdrawing the 500 rupee note. The author says that even the uncertainty spread by such talk can hurt the economy.

In his view, the 2016 decision rested on a basic misunderstanding: that black money means cash. In fact, black income is a flow generated every year, through methods such as fiddling with invoices, while cash is only a small stored part of it. The result is plain to see. According to the Reserve Bank, 99.3 percent of the banned notes came back to the banks, and the windfall of three to four lakh crore rupees that was expected never came.

Large notes made up 86 percent of all cash in circulation at the time, and banks, ATMs and even most ministers had no advance warning. As cash dried up, demand fell, markets went empty, fruit and vegetables rotted in the fields, and milk and tomatoes were dumped on the roads. Small businesses that ran on cash shut down, and workers waited in vain for jobs at labour chowks (roadside spots where daily wage workers gather to be hired).

The author lists how no stated goal was met. The ratio of direct taxes to GDP is stuck around six percent, fake notes were very few to begin with, and the 'cashless' slogan also proved hollow: cash in circulation grew from 18 lakh crore to 43.5 lakh crore rupees, while its share of GDP has stayed at about 12 percent.

Arun Kumar places it in a chain with GST and the 2020 lockdown, where decisions taken without wide consultation broke the unorganised sector. He warns that the push to force small farmers and traders to become 'formal' will turn them into daily wage workers, while in an age of machines the organised sector itself is offering fewer jobs.
nazar: Ten years on, no one has been held accountable for demonetisation, and now there is talk of repeating the same remedy. Those whose income was never black, such as street vendors, small shopkeepers and daily wage workers, paid the highest price. Before any economic decision, it is vital to ask the people who earn and spend in cash every day.
sawal: If 99.3 percent of the notes came back, who was actually caught?
ref: Demonetisation
On 8 November 2016, 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were suddenly declared invalid. Large notes had also been withdrawn once before, in 1978.
Unorganised sector
The part of small business, farming and daily wage work where written contracts, social security and banking are thin and most dealings are in cash.
ank: Banned notes that came back to banks
Share of large notes in cash in circulation

h: Women vote in greater numbers, so why don't they get tickets?
dek: Nandini Raj of ADR uses data to show that parties court women voters but shy away from women candidates.
body: Nandini Raj of the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) writes that 79 years after independence, women's political presence is still mostly for show. In both the 2019 and 2024 Lok Sabha elections, women's turnout was higher than men's, yet only 14 percent of MPs in the 18th Lok Sabha are women.

According to ADR's analysis, of the 51,708 candidates in the 2024 Lok Sabha and assembly elections, only 10 percent were women, and the share is the same among 4,666 MPs and MLAs. Parties say tickets are given on 'winnability', which puts the blame on voters. The author asks why breaking this belief is not the job of party leaders.

Another figure makes the picture clearer. Among women MLAs and MPs, 47 percent come from political families, compared with 18 percent among men. The author says that without family backing, the door to politics is very narrow for a woman, and fear of harassment inside parties narrows it further. In September 2025 the Supreme Court dismissed a plea to bring political parties under the law against sexual harassment at the workplace (POSH).

On the Inter-Parliamentary Union's list of women's share in parliament, India has slipped to 152nd place. The women's reservation law is tied to the census and delimitation, and after the delimitation bill fell in April 2026, it is not expected to take effect before 2034. The author wants reservation delinked from delimitation, POSH applied to parties, and parties to back women who have no political inheritance.
nazar: By reserving half the seats in panchayats (village councils) for women, many states have shown that leadership emerges when given a chance. In Parliament and the assemblies, the same path keeps being put off by some new condition. The habit of treating women only as a vote bank for welfare schemes leaves democracy half complete.
sawal: Why do half of women leaders come from political families?
ref: ADR
Association for Democratic Reforms, a non-governmental group that works on data about elections and candidates.
Women's reservation law
A 2023 law that reserves one third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, but will take effect only after the census and delimitation.

h: Chhath: the Bihari migrant's own ghat
dek: Shreejit Shashwat writes that Chhath kept alive a Bihari identity that faced mockery and contempt, but now wealth and politics have their eyes on it.
body: Writer Shreejit Shashwat, who studied at IIT Delhi, begins with a childhood ache: Karva Chauth appeared again and again on TV and in films, Chhath never did. In his telling, Bihar on screen was either the backdrop for weak stories or a den of jokes and mafia.

The author calls the migration of the 1990s a migration of compulsion. Citing a book by Veena Jha, he notes that between 1991 and 2001 the number of people leaving the state grew by more than 132 percent, and a 2005 World Bank assessment found Bihar's growth well behind the country's. Amid the label of 'labourer', the crude image from Bhojpuri songs and some people's shame about their own roots, Chhath remained the one thing a Bihari is proud of without hesitation.

The author says the beauty of Chhath lies in its simplicity. No priest, no Sanskrit mantras, no idol: the women who keep the fast offer arghya to the sun themselves. At the ghat (riverside steps), people of every caste and class stand side by side, though the author admits caste discrimination still sometimes raises its head. A hundred years ago, labourers who went to the Caribbean and Fiji as girmitiya (indentured workers) took the festival with them, and today Mauritius, Fiji and Suriname stand with India in nominating Chhath to UNESCO.

But the author also fears the new glitter. This year a big film showed Chhath, fulfilling a childhood wish, but private ghats built on rooftops are weakening the sense of community, and Patna's political class seems to encourage them. Meanwhile public ghats are neglected, arrangements for women's safety are weak and the rivers are dirty.
nazar: Chhath is the festival of the migrant worker, for which millions travel home standing in packed trains. Saving it does not mean any identity politics. It means clean rivers, safe ghats and a Bihar that people do not have to flee to earn a living.
sawal: What does a private ghat take away from the shared spirit of Chhath?
ref: Arghya
The ritual of standing in water and offering water or prasad (sacred food) to the setting and rising sun, the heart of Chhath.
Girmitiya
Indian labourers taken on contract to Mauritius, Fiji, Suriname and the Caribbean in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
photo_note: Temples and ghat at Benares, Edwin Lord Weeks

h: Whose police: the law's or those in power?
dek: Former IAS officer Avay Shukla argues that the police have run unchecked over the past decade, and even rebukes from the courts are not stopping them.
body: Retired IAS officer Avay Shukla writes that among the institutions whose credibility has fallen most in the past ten years, the police top the list. In his view, a government that relies on force rather than dialogue makes the police its main tool, and in return the police get a free hand. Each keeps the other alive.

The author lists three symptoms. First, use of force beyond legal limits: cases filed in bulk after the 2020 northeast Delhi riots, most of which did not hold up in court, and harshness against protesters in Niyamgiri and Siang. Citing National Human Rights Commission data, he notes that there were 813 encounter deaths between 2016 and 2022 and not one policeman was punished.

The second symptom is disregard for court orders. The author says that despite clear Supreme Court directions, Delhi Police detained lawyers and journalists during protests, and apologies have now been filed in a contempt case. On 3 November the Allahabad High Court called the state of civil liberties in Uttar Pradesh shameful. The author believes the courts go no further than rebukes, so the fear is gone.

The third symptom, according to the author, is a tilt in part of the force towards the ruling ideology. He points to the force's makeup: OBCs, Dalits and Adivasis (indigenous communities) are 67 percent of the population but 51 percent of the police, women are 10 percent and Muslims just 4 percent. His question is whether any future government, of any ideology, will have the courage to reform the police.
nazar: The Supreme Court's directions on police reform have lain in files for years, and every party, once in power, finds the same police useful. Until encounter killings and custodial deaths are punished and the force reflects the true face of society, the police station will remain a place of fear for ordinary citizens.
sawal: 813 encounter deaths, not one conviction: where is accountability stuck?
ref: Encounter death
A death in an alleged exchange of fire with police or security forces, which requires a magisterial inquiry.
NHRC
National Human Rights Commission, which records and investigates complaints of custodial deaths and police excesses.

h: Bangladesh cannot adapt its way out of the climate crisis
dek: The writers say that after cutting emissions and coping with damage, repairing the atmosphere must become a third pillar, led by the countries hit hardest.
body: An average Bangladeshi emits about 0.6 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, and the country's share of all emissions since the industrial revolution is just 0.11 percent. Yet a 2021 World Bank estimate says that by 2050 nearly two crore (20 million) Bangladeshis may be forced from their homes within their own country because of the climate.

At COP31 under way in Antalya, Turkey, the debate is mostly about money, that is, how much funding comes for cutting emissions and protecting against damage. The writers say these two measures are no longer enough. More than a trillion tonnes of excess carbon has already built up in the atmosphere. Net zero turns off the tap and adaptation mops the floor, but no one drains the water already in the tub.

So they propose a third path: repair. Removing billions of tonnes of carbon each year and holding up the Earth systems that are on the verge of breaking. Disasters cause more than 200 billion dollars of direct losses every year, while a large research programme on this could run on less than one percent of that sum.

The ocean is at the centre of this debate. It has so far absorbed a quarter of all carbon emitted and more than 90 percent of the added heat, but as it warms, this capacity is shrinking. Methods using mangroves, seagrass and seaweed are still raw, and for the writers that is exactly why they should be tested.

Bangladesh has rights over about 1.19 lakh square kilometres of the Bay of Bengal and shares the Sundarbans with India. The writers want the most vulnerable countries to lead such research, so that they are not just receivers of aid but equal partners.
nazar: The other part of the Sundarbans is ours, and the crisis in the Bay is a shared crisis for fishers, honey gatherers and farmers on both sides. If India and Bangladesh come together on this research, it could become new ground for trust between neighbours.
But one caution is needed: in the name of carbon removal, the land and water of coastal communities must not become a testing ground for companies. Their voice should come first in decisions.
sawal: How much say will the Sundarbans' own fishers have in repairing it?
ref: COP31
The 31st annual United Nations climate conference, being held in Antalya, Turkey, in November 2026.
Carbon removal
Taking carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere out through natural or technical means, such as restoring forests and mangroves.

h: The ANC's collapse in South Africa did not happen overnight
dek: A veteran party leader says Nelson Mandela's party fell to 32.5 percent because over three phases it lost growth, then allowed looting, and finally shied away from decisions.
body: In South Africa's 2026 local elections, the African National Congress remained the largest party, but its vote shrank to 32.5 percent. The writer, who has served on the party's executive and twice as ambassador to the United States, says minority voters had already drifted away, and now rural, working class and middle class Black voters have either gone to other parties or stayed home. The decline from 57.5 percent in 2019 has been steady.

Rasool divides it into three phases of nine years each. Under Thabo Mbeki there were weaknesses, but the economy grew at 5.4 percent and in 2006 the party won 65.7 percent of the vote. He calls the Jacob Zuma years a period of ruin, in which, the writer says, state institutions were captured behind the slogan of 'radical economic transformation' and about 500 billion rand was lost.

Cyril Ramaphosa was expected to bring the party back to life. The writer charges that he did no wrong, but also avoided doing right. Tainted people were protected or promoted instead of removed, and Zuma spent only a few hours of his sentence in jail. Zuma's new party gained from this.

Youth unemployment reached 63 percent, but the party did nothing in time about the failure of local bodies. Rasool fears the leadership will now get tangled in blame, denial and bargaining over posts. He suggests the current leadership admit failure, stay until 2027 for stability, and that a transition team rebuild the party before 2029.
nazar: When a party born of a liberation movement starts treating power as its private estate, the first to turn away are the poor in whose name it fought. Against 63 percent youth unemployment, an old legacy is of no use.
There is a lesson here for India too: an identity rooted in the freedom struggle is no guarantee in itself. Trust has to be earned through everyday governance, water, electricity and jobs.
sawal: How was Zuma's 15 month sentence wrapped up in two hours?
ref: African National Congress (ANC)
Nelson Mandela's party, which fought apartheid and has been in power in South Africa since 1994.
State capture
When private interests take hold of state institutions and decisions and run them for their own gain; the Zondo Commission investigated this in the Zuma era.

h: A rush to bind US and Israeli militaries as mandates shift
dek: The writer asks why, when elections in both the US and Israel gave no one a clear mandate, an outgoing Congress is locking in a relationship that will be hard to undo later.
body: Two elections took place eight days apart. On 3 November in the US, Democrats took eight Senate seats to win a 55-44 majority, and the House of Representatives also appears to be going their way. On 27 October in Israel, Netanyahu's Likud became the largest party, but his coalition got stuck at 53 of 120 seats. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, and the president gave Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.

Meanwhile US Secretary of State Rubio said Israel can buy its own weapons and that annual military aid of about 3.8 billion dollars may end soon. The writer says this is not distance, only a change of form: grants are being replaced by joint weapons production and shared technology.

The House passed the defence bill by a slim 216-212, including 750 million dollars for joint programmes with Israel. It also contains a 'defence technology cooperation initiative', which the writer says will move the relationship from open foreign aid into less transparent Pentagon contracts. Republican Thomas Massie and Democrat Ro Khanna tried and failed to remove it.

On the other side, groups linked to the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC spent about 84 million dollars this time, of which about 55 million went on candidates who lost. In one survey, favourable views of Israel among Democrats fell from 52 in 2022 to 30.
The writer argues that passing this provision in the lame-duck session, before the new Congress arrives in January, will close a question that voters have only just opened.
nazar: Amid the destruction of Gaza, joint weapons factories further entrench a war economy whose price is paid by ordinary Palestinians. The changing mood of American voters is opening this debate, and it should not be shut.

India too is expanding its defence partnership with Israel. This piece is a reminder that when such deals move forward through contracts, out of sight of Parliament and the public, accountability is lost.
sawal: Why shouldn't a bill passed 216-212 wait for the new Congress?
ref: Lame-duck session
Sittings of the outgoing US Congress after an election and before new members are sworn in, in which defeated lawmakers also vote.
AIPAC
American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, whose affiliated groups pour heavy money into elections.

h: Two Muslim men killed in police 'encounter' in Nuh, magisterial inquiry ordered
dek: Sabir and Gabbar died in gunfire early on Sunday at a vehicle stopped on suspicion of cattle smuggling; one person is injured.
body: Two young Muslim men were killed by police bullets around 4.30 am on Sunday, 15 November, in Haryana's Nuh district. A team of the Crime Investigation Agency (CIA) of Ferozepur Jhirka, led by Sub-Inspector Mahendra Singh, had received a tip about cattle smuggling and tried to stop a vehicle.

The dead are Sabir of the Ferozepur Jhirka area and Gabbar alias Hadiya, said to be from Rajasthan's Dausa district. Both died at Nalhar Medical College. Tahir of Ghatmika village in Rajasthan's Deeg district is injured and admitted there. Police say a policeman was also hurt.

Police claim the people in the vehicle fired first, after which there was return fire. They say seven cows, three country-made pistols and some cartridges were recovered from a pickup. The report clearly states that these claims have not been independently verified, and the families' side has not yet come out; police only informed them of the deaths.

A Nuh police spokesperson told a news agency that the bodies have been kept in the mortuary and a magisterial inquiry has begun. According to the report, the inquiry will have to establish the circumstances in which shots were fired and whether lethal force was justified. The Mewat region has a long record of violence against Muslim men over cattle-related allegations.
nazar: Every 'encounter' story is printed first in the words of the police and never in the words of the dead. The magisterial inquiry will matter only if ballistic and forensic evidence, the statement of the injured Tahir and the families' account come out in the open.
sawal: When and how will the injured Tahir's statement be recorded in the inquiry?
ref: Magisterial inquiry

An inquiry by an executive magistrate into a police shooting or custodial death.
It is separate from, and considered weaker than, a judicial inquiry.

h: Maharashtra SIR: 99% of voters served notices are back on the rolls
dek: Notices went to 1.2 crore people, but once PAN and Aadhaar were accepted, almost all were added back.
body: Of the 1.2 crore voters sent notices during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll in Maharashtra, more than 99 percent have been added back to the list. Citing Hindustan Times data, Scroll reports that only 72,601 people remain, who either did not submit identity papers or are still being checked.

Notices went out for two reasons. The records of 62.5 lakh people were flagged for 'logical discrepancies', such as differences in the spelling of a parent's name, a very small age gap between parent and child, or having more than six children. 59.7 lakh people could not be linked to the 2002 electoral roll. More than two crore names, or 21.1 percent of the state's voters, had been removed from the draft list of 31 August.

People were able to rejoin when the Election Commission added PAN and Aadhaar to the accepted documents, ended mandatory hearings before booth level officers and allowed papers to be submitted over WhatsApp. Between 31 August and 12 November, 23.6 lakh applications came in, of which 1.2 lakh were Form 7s seeking deletion of names. The final list is due on 30 November.

The report recalls that in May the Supreme Court upheld the process but said deciding citizenship is not the Commission's job. In some BJP-ruled states, people dropped from the list had their ration cards stopped, and in places passport renewals were also held up.
nazar: When the rules were relaxed, 99 percent of the 'suspect' voters turned out to be genuine. This plainly means the problem was not with the people but with the paperwork conditions. In states where these conditions are still strict, the question remains how many genuine voters have been left out.
sawal: Which districts do most of the remaining 72,601 voters come from?
ref: SIR

Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission process in which fresh forms and papers are collected from every voter.
In Maharashtra it was last done in 2002.
Form 7

The form used to file an objection seeking removal of a name from the electoral roll.
Complaints of its misuse have come from several states.

h: 115 foreign speakers at Bharat Summit blocked, MEA calls it a 'sovereign matter'
dek: Visas were cancelled at the Home Ministry's instance after External Affairs Ministry approval, and the government gave no reason.
body: More than a third of the foreign speakers invited to the Congress party's 'Bharat Summit' were stopped from coming to India, even though they had already been cleared. Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, chair of the parliamentary standing committee on external affairs, wrote on 13 November that the External Affairs Ministry had given the green light to 315 speakers, but about 115 of them were refused entry or had their visas cancelled, apparently on the Home Ministry's instructions.

Tharoor said it was not clear under which law the government acted, and at such short notice there was no room to change anything. He said it was a shame that a democracy had become so nervous of critical voices.

When External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked about this at the regular briefing, he said granting visas is a sovereign function of any government. He did not explain why the Home Ministry withdrew permission after the ministry's approval and the visas had been granted.

Among those blocked is Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng, who questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Oslo in May. According to The Wire, she too had received approval and a visa, but before leaving was told the visa had been withdrawn.
nazar: It is easy to dodge accountability by calling something a 'sovereign matter', but when one ministry approves and another quietly reverses it, the country has a right to know why. Blocking a journalist who asked questions deepens that suspicion.
sawal: Under what rule were approved visas later cancelled?
ref: Bharat Summit

An international conference organised by the Congress party, with speakers invited from around the world.
It ended on Saturday, 14 November.

h: AI-altered video of Sushant Singh passed off as Pravin Sawhney
dek: In a clip that spread after the Kulgam attack, the voice calling military operations 'false flag' turned out to be fake.
body: After the terror attack on a CRPF checkpoint in Kulgam, Jammu and Kashmir, on 11 November, a video began circulating on social media. It was claimed that former army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney was calling the Kulgam action, the Balakot strike and Operation Sindoor 'false flag operations' carried out for political gain.

Alt News's check found two things. First, the man in the video is not Pravin Sawhney but columnist Sushant Singh; the interviewer even calls him 'Sushant'. Second, the lip movements and voice do not match and the delivery is flat and mechanical, common signs of an AI-generated voice.

Sushant Singh himself said on X on 13 November that the video was made with AI. He also shared a link to the real interview, posted on The Wire's YouTube channel in March 2025. Comparing the two, the clothes, background and lighting were identical; only the voice had been changed. The real conversation does not even mention Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot or 'false flag'; there Singh was talking about civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
The clip began spreading on 12 November from a handle on X and then reached several other accounts and Facebook pages on South Asian geopolitics.
nazar: Putting invented words in the mouth of a critical journalist right after an attack is not just a lie; it is groundwork for branding him a traitor. AI has made this cheap, so tracing the source of every sensational clip before passing it on is now a civic duty.
sawal: Which parts of the real interview were kept exactly the same in the fake clip?
ref: False flag

An act carried out by someone in order to pin it on someone else.
The term is often used in conspiracy claims.
Deepfake
Video or audio made or altered with AI, in which a person appears to say what they never said.

h: Adani affidavit cut project cost by 99%, and the tiger reserve's share with it
dek: Showing the cost of the Tarli pumped storage project in Satara as 56.75 crore instead of 5,675 crore reduced conservation dues by about 225 crore rupees.
body: Adani Green Energy wants to build a 1,500 megawatt pumped storage project on the Tarli dam in Patan tehsil of Maharashtra's Satara district. The site, covering 150.74 hectares of land in four villages, Nivade, Tondoshi, Kalambe and Jalu, falls in the notified eco-sensitive zone of the Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary, which is part of the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve.

In a February 2025 letter from the Environment Ministry, its cost was recorded as 5,675 crore rupees. The State Wildlife Board set a condition that 4 percent of the cost, about 227 crore rupees, be deposited with the tiger reserve. But on 8 September a company official put the cost at just 56.75 crore rupees in a notarised affidavit, and on 12 October the forest department demanded 56.75 lakh rupees on that basis, which was paid.

Satara's honorary wildlife warden Rohan Bhate complained on 30 October that this had wrongly reduced the conservation share by about 225 crore rupees. On 6 November the Union Environment Ministry asked the state to investigate on priority. Now the state's Principal Chief Conservator of Forests says the revised figure had not been accepted, which contradicts his own October letter.

The company calls the allegations misleading. It says 56.75 crore was only the cost of investigation and surveys, and that the project is on private land outside the protected area, though older forest department letters place it in the sensitive zone. The Congress has repeated its demand for a Joint Parliamentary Committee probe.
nazar: The tiger forest's share fell to a hundredth through a single affidavit and the forest department took the money without question. This points less to a mistake than to how the system is built. The probe should reach not only the company but also the officials who gave approval.
sawal: On what basis did the forest department accept the reduced cost on 12 October?
ref: Pumped storage
A way of storing electricity: cheap power is used to pump water uphill, and when needed it is released downhill to generate electricity.
Eco-sensitive zone
The belt around sanctuaries where large construction faces restrictions and extra conditions.

h: Resettled by the government after the 1983 riots, now uprooted by it
dek: Bulldozers ran over the 'Muslim camp' settlement in Bogeenadi PGR in Assam's Lakhimpur, and along with the homes a mosque built on land sanctioned in 1992 was also demolished.
body: On Friday the Lakhimpur district administration in Assam ran an eviction drive in the Bogeenadi PGR area and demolished the homes of Bengali Muslim families whom the government itself had settled there four decades ago. Revenue officials, with a heavy security force, arrived in the morning at the 'Muslim camp' settlement near Bogeenadi police station and the weekly market. According to the report, about 320 hectares of land were cleared in the drive.

These families were uprooted in the 1983 violence at Bhimpora-Bodhakora during the Assam agitation, when a mob attacked Bhimpora village. They were first given shelter at the police station, then at the market, and later the administration gave them PGR land. Their identity cards were made here in June 1983. Since 2008 the settlement had a primary school, an anganwadi (childcare) centre, a Jal Jeevan Mission water pipeline and even electricity connections. Government papers list it under names such as 'Refugee Camp', 'Muslim Camp' and 'Miya Camp'.

The settlement's mosque was also demolished in the eviction. According to a government letter of 25 September 1992 held by residents, land for the mosque and graveyard had been formally allotted. Residents allege that parts of the PGR occupied by other communities nearby were spared. Protesting women said they would not leave their homes. Affected families have asked the government for alternative rehabilitation. The action follows drives in Nagaon, Hojai, Golaghat and Dhubri, which Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has called 'cleaning the house'.
nazar: Turning people whom the state rescued from violence and gave identity cards, a school, water and electricity into 'encroachers' on that same land is a question not of law but of intent. If other occupations nearby really were spared, this is not eviction but selective punishment, and making people homeless a second time without rehabilitation is an open disregard of Article 21 of the Constitution.
sawal: How did mosque land allotted in 1992 become illegal?
ref: PGR

Professional Grazing Reserve, government land in Assam set aside for grazing cattle.
Eviction drives often target settlements on these lands.

h: 40 religious leaders fast in Leh as Apex Body insists winter polls be put off
dek: The Leh Apex Body's sit-in and relay hunger strike go on, and the Centre has hinted at talks after the election.
ask: Resume the talks, put off the hill council polls during winter
body: In Ladakh, the Leh Apex Body (LAB) has taken its movement a step further. A relay hunger strike began on Saturday, with 40 religious leaders keeping a 24-hour fast. LAB president Chering Dorjay Lakruk was among them. Before this, a peaceful sit-in has been going on since Thursday at NDS Memorial Park in Leh, led by Lakruk himself.

According to Lakruk, word has come through informal channels that the Centre is ready for talks at the level of the high-powered committee between 5 and 10 December, after the 4 December hill council (LAHDC) election. The government has not officially confirmed this.

The LAB is questioning the timing of the election. Lakruk says this will be the first election in Ladakh's history held in the harsh winter, when about a quarter of the population lives outside the region. He alleges that names have been struck off the voter list on a large scale, many young people have been left out and the names of dead people are still listed. He says the LAB is not against the election, it only wants it put off until people return and the list is corrected.

The movement's demands include the Centre restarting talks on constitutional safeguards and statehood, and an elected body headed by a chief minister. Jharkhand's tribal welfare minister came to the protest site to express support. Lakruk has said both the sit-in and the hunger strike will go on until the demands are met.
nazar: Even after the restrictions on Sonam Wangchuk, the movement in Leh has reached the point of religious leaders fasting. That shows the issue is not about one face but about the whole region. Offering talks only after the election, and saying nothing officially, is no way to build trust.
sawal: When a quarter of the people are away, whose vote will this be?
ref: Leh Apex Body
A platform of religious, social and political groups in Leh, which, together with the Kargil Democratic Alliance, is demanding statehood and Sixth Schedule protection for Ladakh.
LAHDC
Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council, the elected hill councils of Leh and Kargil, which hold powers over local development.

h: Death in custody in Karnal, family refuses body until arrests
dek: After the death of Jitender of Bijna village, his family and community blocked roads, and a case was filed against six policemen.
ask: Arrest all the accused policemen, preserve the CCTV footage
body: The mood in Karnal, Haryana, was tense on Sunday. After the alleged death in police custody of 30-year-old Jitender of Bijna village, his family, relatives, villagers and members of the Rajput community blocked a road in the city. They said they would not take the body from the post-mortem house of Kalpana Chawla Medical College until all the accused policemen were arrested.

According to the complaint by Jitender's brother Shubham Singh, a CIA-2 team picked him up from home on the morning of 11 November. The family says they were not told where he was, so on 12 November they filed a petition in the High Court. On 13 November they were allowed to meet him, and he looked fine then. But they allege the family was made to sign blank papers and pressured to withdraw the petition. On 14 November they got news of his death through the sarpanch (village head).

Police have registered a case under several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including murder, against six personnel, among them CIA-2 in-charge Inspector Parveen Sharma and Head Constable Sandeep. A judicial inquiry has begun, and the post-mortem was done by a board of doctors under a magistrate's supervision. Protesters raised questions, fearing that the names of other policemen were being hidden and the footage tampered with. In the evening, Assandh MLA Yogender Rana and DSP Gorakhpal Rana assured them that everyone would be arrested, and the family then agreed to take the body on Monday morning.
nazar: The family went all the way to the High Court over his disappearance, and still the man died in custody. That is the most serious part. The FIR is a first step. The real test will be whether arrests happen, or the case gets buried in a departmental inquiry.
sawal: Despite the court stepping in, why was Jitender missing for three days?
ref: CIA
District units of the Haryana Police's Crime Investigation Agency, which investigate and interrogate in serious crimes.
Inquiry into custodial death
By law, every such death must be inquired into by a judicial magistrate, with a video-recorded post-mortem.

h: Song dam displaced on sit-in for four days, warn of road blockade
dek: Top of the 15-point demands of the affected people, sitting in two villages of Tehri and Dehradun, is land in return for land.
ask: Land for land, residential plots and a job for every family
body: In Uttarakhand, the sit-in by villagers who are being uprooted or affected by the Song dam project has reached its fourth day. The villagers are sitting in Saudna village in the Dhanaulti assembly constituency and Hilaswali village in the Raipur assembly constituency. Ravindra Singh Panwar, president of the Song Dam Affected and Displaced Committee, and secretary Balveer Singh Kandari say that in all these days no one from the government or administration has come to check on them.

The committee has 15 demands. They include land in return for the land being taken, plots to live on, a job for one member of every displaced and affected family, and roads and bridges in the project area.

The villagers say the administration had ended their protest once before with assurances, but those promises were never acted on, so they have had to sit in again. Now they have warned that if concrete action is not taken soon, they will block roads at Maldevta, the area's market, and at Raipur Chowk. Among the many villagers at the sit-in are Vikram Singh Kandari, Raviraj Panwar, Dipendra Kothari, Devendra Negi and Anand Negi.
nazar: In the hills, the burden of a dam always falls on the villages that have nothing but their farms. Ending a sit-in with assurances and then forgetting about it is exactly the cycle that pushes movements to blocking roads.
sawal: In which file are last time's assurances stuck?
ref: Song dam project
A proposed dam on the Song river in Dehradun district, meant to bring drinking water to Dehradun city by gravity.
Land for land
The demand of displaced people that instead of cash compensation they get the same amount of farmable land, so their livelihood survives.

h: Women take to the streets in Sagar's Machharyai after liquor death
dek: The day after 35-year-old Vishnu died, women demanded the liquor shop be removed from their residential neighbourhood.
ask: Remove the liquor shop from the residential area
body: In the Machharyai area of Sagar city in Madhya Pradesh, women came out on the street on Sunday and demanded that the neighbourhood's liquor shop be removed. A day earlier, on Saturday, Vishnu, the 35-year-old son of Rajaram Khatik, died after drinking liquor from this same shop, and another young man was admitted to hospital in a serious condition.

The women say the shop is in a residential area and has spoiled the atmosphere of the whole locality. Drunk men create a ruckus late into the night, gambling goes on, and it has become hard for women and girls to walk down the lane. This is affecting children and families.

Police and officials reached the spot, tried to calm the women and heard them out. The women handed over a memorandum and warned that if the shop is not removed, the protest will grow. Congress city president Mahesh Jatav met the family, called the death the result of the administration's negligence, and demanded testing of liquor samples, action against those responsible and compensation of one crore rupees for the family. Jatav alleges that in the past four or five days there have been reports of illness and death from liquor in several nearby areas.
nazar: Where a liquor shop will open is often decided without asking the women who pay its price every day. Accepting a memorandum after a death is not enough. Testing the liquor and deciding on the shop's location can no longer be put off.
sawal: Whose approval got the shop in the neighbourhood its licence?
ref: Spurious liquor
Liquor mixed with methyl alcohol, which can cause blindness and even death; in such cases lab testing of samples is crucial.

h: Valarmathi on hunger strike for 20 days in Thiruvananthapuram, CM agrees to talks
dek: Candidates on the LPST rank list continue their sit-in outside the Secretariat, with no date fixed for talks yet.
ask: Fill all vacancies before the list expires
body: Candidates on the Lower Primary School Teacher (LPST) rank list, sitting in protest outside the Kerala Secretariat, were told on Sunday that Chief Minister V D Satheesan will discuss their demands with Education Minister N Samsudheen. The date and time of the meeting have not been announced yet, so the candidates have said the sit-in will go on until they get a firm assurance.

S Valarmathi, secretary of the All Kerala LPST Rank Holders Association, has been on an indefinite fast since 26 October, with her head shaved. On 11 November, Cantonment police removed the protesters and tore down their shed, but they came back the next morning. On 12 November doctors found low sodium in her body and irregularities in her ECG, after which she was admitted to the ICU of the General Hospital.

The candidates' demands are: fill all current vacancies before the list expires, extend the list's validity, cut the teacher-student ratio in lower classes from 1:30 to 1:25, bring appointments in aided schools and headmaster posts under the PSC, and save the posts being lost as divisions shrink.
nazar: Having to fast for a job even after passing the exam and making the list is a failure of the recruitment system. For a candidate who has already ended up in the ICU, a promise of talks without a date is far too little.
sawal: Why did a candidate who passed have to shave her head for a job?
ref: Rank list
The list of qualified candidates drawn up after a Public Service Commission exam, from which appointments are made only until a fixed expiry date.

h: 24-hour shutdown across Manipur over killing of four civilians in Ukhrul
dek: Indigenous groups appealed for a peaceful shutdown and asked the governments for safety and justice.
ask: Protect people travelling on the national highway and act against the killers
body: In Manipur's Ukhrul district, four Naga civilians, two of them women, were killed on 13 November in an ambush on National Highway 202 near New Haven. They were reportedly travelling towards Imphal in two vehicles.

In protest against the killings, the Native People's Committee, Manipur, along with civil society groups of the hills and the valley, announced a statewide general strike from midnight of 15 November to midnight of 16 November. Shops, markets, private offices, schools and colleges were asked to stay shut and vehicles to stay off the roads, while hospitals, ambulances, fire services, water, electricity and the media were exempted. The group appealed to people to observe the shutdown peacefully and keep up communal harmony.

The Tangkhul Naga Long held an emergency meeting with groups from its area and gave the state and central governments three days. It demands that the National Investigation Agency probe the case and that action be taken against armed groups said to be active in Naga areas. A day earlier, on 12 November, Newton Mahung, a 49-year-old farmer from Sinakeithei village, was shot while harvesting paddy. The attackers have not yet been officially identified.
nazar: When in Manipur even going out on the road or harvesting paddy in a field means risking your life, the peaceful shutdown and appeal for harmony by civil groups is the voice of a state that has paid the highest price for violence. The responsibility lies with the government: secure the highway, hold a fair investigation, and give equal justice to the dead of every community, so that one killing does not become the excuse for the next.
sawal: After repeated attacks on Highway 202, why is there still no protection?
ref: Native People's Committee, Manipur
A platform of civil society groups of Manipur's indigenous communities, and the organiser of this shutdown.
Tangkhul Naga Long
The apex social body of the Tangkhul Naga community of the Ukhrul region, which speaks to the government on the community's behalf.

h: A machine that listened for tigers, stalled for lack of money
dek: In Nepal's Bardiya, a cheap technology built on the alarm calls of deer and monkeys warned villages, then stopped for want of resources.
body: In south-western Nepal, people in the villages around Bardiya National Park know how to read the language of the forest. When chital deer, rhesus monkeys and langurs suddenly start shrieking, people understand that a tiger or leopard is somewhere close. Along with pugmarks and droppings, these sounds tell them when it is not safe to go into the forest.

Building on this local knowledge, an experiment ran in the Dalla community forest from December 2024 to March 2025. Solar-powered sound recorders were fixed on trees, each costing about 50 dollars. An AI model recognised the animals' alarm calls and automatically sent a message saying which area the predator might be in.

The problem is not a small one. Nepal's count of wild tigers has reached a record 429, and 112 of them are around Bardiya. According to a recent study, tigers attacked people 245 times between 2010 and 2024, and 141 people lost their lives.

Thengchu Tharu, a 60-year-old forest guard of the Dalla community forest, said the machine's warnings matched the signs seen on the ground. He says if people know in advance, they simply do not need to go that way. Bhadai Tharu, chair of the neighbouring Gauri community forest, has himself survived a tiger attack.

According to Casey Anderson, the American wildlife filmmaker who led the experiment, the project stopped for lack of money, staff and local institutional support, and the team took its equipment to India. Sabnam Pathak of Nepal's Department of Forests and Soil Conservation says any new tool needs long testing before it is adopted on a large scale. This report is a summary of a detailed October report by Praveen Kumar Yadav.
nazar: The rising number of tigers is a conservation success, but its price is paid by Tharu families living at the forest's edge. A technology built on their own knowledge, and cheap too, could not get a few hundred dollars and a little government support to keep running. That shows village safety is still not a priority.
sawal: Whose job is it, finally, to run a fifty-dollar machine?
ref: Community forest

Forests in Nepal handed over to local user groups.
The villagers themselves set the rules for their care and use.
Tharu

An indigenous community living in the Terai of Nepal and India.
Their settlements at the edge of forests like Bardiya are centuries old.

h: The screen hero has no job, the worker has no voice in literature
dek: Santosh Kumar's new column, Shramik Sansar (The Workers' World), asks where the working person has vanished to in Hindi stories and poems.
body: Santosh Kumar is a biostatistician by profession and also a trade union activist. His fortnightly column on Sammukh, Shramik Sansar, begins with this piece, and it opens with a pointed question: what work do today's film heroes actually do? The writer says the new-age hero is glamorous but is hardly ever seen earning a living, while the worker is either made the villain, or called a 'beneficiary' in government language and a 'troublemaker' in media language.

A comparison with old Hindi cinema makes this clearer. In Naya Daur (New Age), Dilip Kumar drove a tonga (horse cart), in Do Bigha Zamin (Two Acres of Land), Balraj Sahni pulled a rickshaw, and Amol Palekar's characters were ordinary clerks. Back then, work was part of the hero's identity. The writer says mainstream Hindi literature too has shied away from fatigue and sweat and shrunk into a decorative sense of beauty.

He then takes us around the traditions across the world where workers write for themselves: Marathi poet Narayan Surve, Iranian construction worker Sabir Haka, China's 'dagong' literature and Foxconn's worker-poet Xu Lizhi, and South Africa's worker-bards. In India he recalls the Dalit Panthers, Namdeo Dhasal and Omprakash Valmiki's Joothan (Leftovers), where the exploitation of caste and of labour were recorded together.

The piece's most useful distinction is that even excellent books like those of Neha Dixit or Aman Sethi were written by looking at the worker from outside, whereas Surve or Xu Lizhi speak in their own voice. The writer says literature written by workers themselves is still very scarce in India.

His conclusion is that the debate is not about style but about how we see: who is considered worth listening to, and whose testimony is treated as mere 'raw material'. He appeals to publishers, magazines and readers to bring down these walls.
nazar: This column catches a void we see every day but never name. Gig workers, construction workers, sanitation workers: they all keep the city running, but lines written by them are hard to find in Hindi magazines. If literature wants to be democratic, it has to give the worker room to be a writer, not just a subject.
sawal: Which magazine will print the poetry of the man selling ice at Jantar Mantar?
ref: Dagong literature

Literature written by migrant factory workers in China who came from villages to cities.
Poets like Xu Lizhi, who wrote about life on the assembly line, became its face.
Dalit Panthers

A militant organisation of Dalit youth founded in Mumbai in 1972.
Poets like Namdeo Dhasal changed the language of Marathi poetry through it.

h: A little distance in marriage, so both can breathe
dek: The new instalment of Pallavi Vinod's Dampatya (Married Life) series asks why living together turns into keeping watch on each other.
body: Fiction writer Pallavi Vinod is writing a series of essays on married relationships on Sammukh, called Dampatya. The subject of this instalment is distance, meaning the personal space that keeps a relationship alive, and which most couples either wipe out completely or handle the wrong way.

It opens with a singer named Mangala, who gave up singing a few months after her wedding. At her in-laws' home her music was praised at first, but when she started her riyaz (daily practice) again, the family's unease filled her with guilt. Slowly her confidence broke, responsibilities grew, and there was neither time nor space left for her art.

The writer draws an interesting comparison: brothers and sisters get separate rooms as they grow up, but husband and wife are expected to share the room, the passwords and everything else. In her view, personal space does not mean separate beds, but the freedom to read, meet friends or follow a hobby without suspicion. Advice may be given, but not imposed.

She uses an experience of her own to show that the all-day questioning of 'where are you, what are you doing' looks like love from outside but really becomes mutual surveillance. In old-style homes, husbands get lost in their phones and the TV, and the wife, worn out by housework, goes unseen. This very neglect later turns into watchfulness.
The essay stresses the difference that freedom and emotional distance are not the same thing. Giving a partner space matters, but being there when needed matters even more.
nazar: Mangala's story is not about one home. In India, the talent of millions of women quietly shuts down after marriage in the name of 'peace at home', and no one even counts it as a loss. This essay opens up that silence in everyday language, without preaching.
sawal: In which corner might Mangala's tanpura be lying now?
ref: Dampatya series

A series of essays by Pallavi Vinod on Sammukh.
Each instalment takes up one tension or question within marriage.

h: A Marathi circus caught in the war in Burma
dek: A review of Vishwas Patil's novel The Great Kanchana Circus: a powerful story, but weighed down by detail.
body: Marathi writer Vishwas Patil's novel has now come out in English, translated by Nadeem Khan and published by Westland. Debasmita Bhowmik has reviewed it on Scroll, and her verdict is mixed: a terrific premise, but an exhausting execution.

The story is about a small travelling circus set up by Sarang Shinde, back from the army, with his daughter Kanchana. Touring Maharashtra and Karnataka, the circus makes a name, and Kanchana, with her risky acts alongside her tigress, becomes its heart. The first part is about the father-daughter bond, and about how Sarang, rejected by his family and community, raised his daughter alone. The reviewer says this part drags because of flashbacks and repetition.

In the second part, the circus reaches Burma at the start of the Second World War. Christmas earnings are good, but then Japanese bombing begins, and performers, workers and animals are all stranded there. Amid the British retreat, the dangerous journey home falls on Kanchana's shoulders.

Bhowmik praises Patil's research. While working on a biography of Subhas Chandra Bose, he came across a mention of the circus in accounts of the British retreat, and later spoke to old circus performers. The depiction of ethnic tensions in Burma and hatred against successful Indian traders is also powerful.

But her complaint is that the details smother the story, and the prose becomes almost like a report. The ease with which the care of animals is shown seems odd to her against today's debates on animal welfare.
nazar: The story of the lakhs of Indians who walked back from Burma during the Second World War is barely there in our books. A Marathi novel reaching this forgotten exodus through translation is a good example of bridges between Indian languages, even if the book lacks tightness.
sawal: Which route would Kanchana have taken home with her tigress, amid the bombing?
ref: The 1942 Burma exodus

After the Japanese attack, lakhs of Indians returned from Burma to India on foot and by boat.
Thousands died on the way from hunger and disease.

h: Booker-winning novel: when the seams of reality start to come apart
dek: Tim Jarvis sees M. John Harrison's The End of Everything as a marvel of weird fiction for unsettled times.
body: This year's Booker Prize has gone to British writer M. John Harrison's novel The End of Everything. This piece by Tim Jarvis, who teaches creative writing at Anglia Ruskin University, was originally written for The Conversation and published on Scroll.

On the surface the frame is familiar: an alien invasion. Humans are fighting an inconclusive war with beings called the 'iGhetti', whose name is a dig at a famous tech company's naming style. In Britain they are mostly confined to London's financial district, but their traces turn up all over the world: biological gadgets, self-shaping objects and 'bad patches' where reality seems to come apart. On the Kent coast, Philip Tennant finds one such thing, which slowly begins to take human shape, and he sets off on a strange journey with his forgetful aunt Marnie.

According to Jarvis, a summary of the plot does not capture the book's strength. Harrison himself has long held that plot is a poor substitute for story. The prose is fragmentary but not scattered, and a shocking event near the end splits the novel in two, with the second half moving from grief towards acceptance.

The piece places Harrison in the tradition of the 'weird', where horror, fantasy and early science fiction blend together. The term 'New Weird' was also coined by him. Jarvis sees it as a response to an age of economic instability, climate crisis and artificial intelligence.
Despite its bleak world, he says, the book is built on a slow but deep hope.
nazar: In an age of climate crisis and machines intruding more and more, realist frames often fall short. Hindi and Urdu too have old ground for fantasy and weird fiction, from the dastan (oral epic tale) to the experiments of the Nayi Kahani (New Story) movement. This prize is a reminder that even a story that seems absurd can tell the truth of its time.
sawal: If something found on the seashore started becoming human, what would we ask?
ref: New Weird

A strand of fiction that emerged in the late twentieth century, mixing horror, fantasy and science fiction.
China Miéville is one of its best-known writers.
Booker Prize
Britain's prestigious annual literary prize for a novel published in English.

h: Why should a writer worry about the world? Ashok Vajpeyi answers
dek: In Kabhi-Kabhar (Now and Then), Vajpeyi says caring about the world is not a writer's excess but the very ground of the craft.
body: Ashok Vajpeyi's weekly column Kabhi-Kabhar begins this time with a conversation. An acquaintance asked him why writers worry so much about the world, when that is the job of politicians, social workers, economists and scholars. A writer should stick to his language and his medium, and too much worrying only eats up energy.

Vajpeyi thinks the objection is worth considering, but calls it wrong. In his view, the world is at the very centre of literature. Great writers do not turn away from the world. They look at it through their imagination, and often create a counter-world. Literature does not give solutions, it raises questions, but it widens the map of empathy and makes society aware of its own complexity. Often it senses the coming times early and acts as a moral watchman, even if society does not listen.

In the second part he turns to the present situation. In his view, some people are profiting from this atmosphere, but for many it is unbearable. He asks citizens to speak up for the Constitution and its values, and praises the recent non-violent youth protests. He cites Salman Rushdie's point that poetry cannot stop a bullet, but a writer can tell the truth and name the lie.
Vajpeyi stresses the special responsibility of the Hindi belt, where, in his view, lies, communal hatred and mob violence are the most widespread.
The last part of the column is about Anupam Sud's large exhibition at the National Gallery of Modern Art in Delhi, whose women are images not of defeat but of endurance.
nazar: In Hindi, the advice to 'stay away from politics' often comes dressed as neutrality. Vajpeyi's argument cuts straight through that illusion. In a region where hatred is becoming the language of everyday life, a writer's silence is also taking a side.
sawal: What will a writer of the Hindi belt say to the mob in his own neighbourhood?
ref: Kabhi-Kabhar

Ashok Vajpeyi's long-running weekly column.
It brings together comments on literature, art and public life.
Anupam Sud

A senior painter and printmaker from Delhi.
Human figures, especially women, are at the centre of her work.

h: Gandhi in '47: celebrations in Delhi, an old man in Calcutta
dek: Manoj Kumar Jha reviews Pushya Mitra's book Gandhi ka Saintalis (Gandhi's Forty-Seven), which looks at Gandhi's last year through a human eye.
body: Journalist Pushya Mitra's book Gandhi ka Saintalis: Ishwar Allah Tero Naam (Gandhi's Forty-Seven: Ishwar and Allah Are Your Names) has been published by Rajkamal Prakashan. Reviewing it on The Wire Hindi, Manoj Kumar Jha first puts his finger on a common habit: we either make Gandhi a god or erase him from history, and either way we lose the human being who grappled with the moral challenges of his time.

The reviewer recalls his student days, when Sumit Sarkar's Modern India introduced him to the Gandhi of Noakhali: an old man without army, police or power, walking through riot-scorched villages and listening to people's grief. Later, reading Sudhir Chandra and Pyarelal deepened this interest.

In his view, Pushya Mitra's method is that of storytelling. Here history is made of voices, fear, suspicion and hatred, and also of the compassion that somehow survived among them. The book moves through Noakhali, Bihar, Calcutta and Delhi, and asks what kept Gandhi going while the leaders were busy with the transfer of power.

At its centre is 15 August 1947. Delhi was celebrating freedom and Gandhi was in riot-ravaged Calcutta. Jha believes his absence from the capital says more than his presence would have. He also underlines that Gandhi did not practise selective morality: he stood up in the same way for Hindus in Noakhali and for Muslims in Bihar.
The review accepts that many of Gandhi's decisions are open to debate, but his last phase shows that his principles were not mere sermons.
nazar: Today our response to violence often depends on who the killer is and who the victim is. Gandhi's forty-seven is a reminder of the standard by which the wrongs of one's own community are called out just as firmly. The Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb (shared Hindu-Muslim culture) rested on this courage, and still does.
sawal: What was Gandhi's distance from Delhi on Independence Day saying?
ref: Noakhali

A district in present-day Bangladesh that saw terrible communal violence in 1946.
Gandhi spent months walking from village to village there, working for peace.
